utterances.text: Well, naturally that's what I expected, that's what I saw, that's what I obtained; and this was a sign that indicated to me that what I was asking for was -- what I was waiting for, that I actually got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take you back to your testimony in June this year and read you a question and answer that was put to you on this same topic. Now, in cross-examination you were asked: "The documents you got from the Hotel Fontana, did they indicate that Vujadin Popovic had spent the night there in July any time 1995?" And this was your answer: "The documents existed. I didn't go into the contents of the documents. The most important thing was that the documents date from the month of July 1995 and that they related to that particular lodging. I didn't have any need to go into the contents of your documents, to be able to answer your question." Now, sir, which of your testimony under oath is correct, the one from June or the one from today?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the sense remains the same, both times. Now, if you want to define what it means that I didn't go into the contents, I think that there was the first name and the last name in some of the documents on some of the invoices, several invoices indicating that Vujadin Popovic spent the night in the hotel two times. What does it mean that I wasn't going into the substance - and now I'm saying that I just browsed through the invoices - I meant the same thing. That this information exists there. It is recorded that this man did spend the night in the hotel. So there is a record of it. I think the essence is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a specific question in June. Did those documents indicate that Vujadin Popovic had spent the night there in July 1995? And you, your response was that you didn't have any need to go into the content. Today, you told us that you did see his name on those documents. That's a different answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My friend missed one sentence from previously cited -- a previously cited passage that he said the document existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 46, line 14, "the document existed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the previous page on 14, I've read -- that's been read into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 46, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "The documents existed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's what I read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, did any of the material you saw contain the name "Beara"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed with this question because we want to see clear on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered that previous question. So let's go through that first, and then you proceed with this Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My question was, sir, you were asked in your testimony in June whether the documents you saw indicated that Vujadin Popovic had spent the night there in July of 1995. The version you gave today was very different from the version you gave then. Now, which of your testimony is correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to give the same answer both then and now. I claimed that Vujadin Popovic was listed in the document. His name was there. The date when he stayed there and other information that was listed there, the sum of money and so on. So I saw that the moment I received the documents, and I think that today I gave the same answer to the effect that I saw that Popovic was listed as a guest in the hotel on those dates. So that was not only one night but several or more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, did any of the material you saw contain the name "Beara"?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a new question for me. In the documents that I received from Ilic, I did not find Beara's name. If I had, I would have returned the documents to him. What would I do with a document that nobody needs and that I, myself, don't need. So I really have to say no. Why would I be looking for other names, other persons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So the Bratunac Brigade authorisations that you fail to mention in June, you didn't see Mr. Beara's name on one of them?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite specific, the authorisations or approvals from the Bratunac Brigade, I didn't see Mr. Beara's name at all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you look at these authorisations?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, several times. I know them by heart. Of course, when I receive something then I go through all the pages, I look at the format, I check whether there are any duplicates or forgeries. I look for anything that I may have been planted there, anything that is out of the ordinary in terms of bookkeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I only have one more question to you -- question for you. What happened to the documents that Mr. Zivanovic lost in 2006? Have those documents ever been found?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I handed over to him another set of documents, the same documents, I have to say. Now, as to what happened with the previous set I did not discuss this with him. I didn't even ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So do you know where these -- the missing documents, where were they last seen?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: When I handed over the documents the first time in Zvornik, I was not aware of what happened with them at all up until the time when I was told that I should go back to the hotel and obtain them once again. So as for their fate, I didn't inquire about that and I was not interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Prost would like to put some questions to you, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, I am going to begin with something you just answered to Mr. Mitchell because I am not clear at all now on what kind of a review you made of these documents. Now, Mr. Mitchell noted your testimony before us previously, and this is at page 21944, where you said that, in answer to the question about Mr. Popovic, you said: "I didn't go into the content of the documents. The important thing was that the documents dated from the month of July and they related to that particular lodging. I didn't have any need to go into the contents of the documents." Now, today, earlier on, you said something very similar. You said that when you received - and this was at page 31, lines 1 to 15 - when you received these documents the first time, you said: "I just browsed through the documents superficially. I didn't count them." You've indicated you didn't list them. And yet, just now, at page 49, you say, in terms of the authorisations, which were in those documents: "I know them by heart. When I receive something, I go through all the pages. I look at the format. I check whether there are duplicates or forgeries. I look for anything that may have been planted there, anything out of ordinary in terms of bookkeeping." So tell me, what is the situation, did you review these documents in detail or did you not?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the moment when I received the documents is one thing, and the other thing is the period when I was in possession of the those documents up until the time when I handed them over to Mr. Zivanovic. Given the circumstances at the time when Ilic handed those documents to me, Ilic simply went out into the street and I could not do all those things that you just mentioned here. But throughout the period while I was in possession of those documents, well, I had them in my custody, up until the time when I handed them over to Defence counsel, I had an opportunity to go through them in detail. Did I that for my own sake. So I don't know if you understand me or not, so I did not have them in my possession for just a day or two; and they were not just kept somewhere. I had to familiarise myself with them and to be able to convey properly the quality of the work, whether everything that was requested was indeed present. All the things that were present, the quantity, the contents, I had to specify all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Well, that's quite different then from what you told us in June because there was no specification on that question as to the time-period. You were asked about the content of the documents and you seem to indicate previously that you had not looked at the content. But now you're telling us that you did do a very thorough review of the contents of these documents. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asked the question at the time. I wasn't asked up until now to provide this extent of explanation as I am being asked now. They only asked whether I inspected these documents and then we moved on. There was no time for me to explain. I do have the time now to talk about document numbers, are these incidence voice, are these authorisations, and so on and so forth, discussing the type of document. But back then it was just one thing of many that were discussed. I was asked to say specifically what I did in that building during those days, what I sought and what I received. That was the only purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And when you did this examination, then, did you make a list as might be normal for an investigator, list out what the documents were, what the dates were, what the contents were? Did you make a list of that nature to give over to Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever there were situations like that, and there were quite a number of them, I never put together an attachment like that specifying these things. I never attached any document to the documents that I had singled out. I would get the documents. I would put them in an envelope. In this case -- even that was not the case, there was no envelope involved; and then I would deliver them like that to the counsel with no signatures and no receipts or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to be very specific here since we've had some confusion on the point. We are not talking about whether you made a list right at the time that you received the documents, but when you did this thorough review that you just told us about, did you during the course of that review make any kind of a list of the documents that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And did you take any notes about the contents of those documents? Did you keep any notes whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And afterwards, at any point in time, and I don't want to be limited in any time-frame here, did you at any point in time make a list of those document or make notes about the contents of those documents, anything of that nature, at any time?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, not then, not ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Based on that, you testified here today, in summary you had no list; and you obviously didn't keep any copies of these documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Are you suggesting that I -- or are you asking me whether I made copies of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you whether you made any copies.

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Why would I have? I do apologise, but why would I have done anything like that? Perhaps to keep those, but for what purpose? I had no use for those, I would just pass them along so that they might be used wherever necessary. I certainly didn't need to keep those at my home. I didn't copy them. I didn't make any copies or distribute copies. There is a certain procedure in place for things like these and the procedure is known to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay then. I want to try and understand your answer to this question earlier, which is Mr. Zivanovic put to you that, "Today," and I am going to read from his question: "Today in my office I showed you a selection of documents that the OTP had obtained, and I read to you part of the statement given by --" I believe it was Gallagher, "The OTP investigator," miss, it should be: "Who interviewed Mr. Brana Ilic about inter alia this handover of documents. I showed you these documents that Mr. Ilic mentioned, tell me when you compared those documents and the documents that you received, can you tell me whether these are two identical sets of documents and if -- if there are any differences what the differences are?" And your answer was: "These two sets of documents are identical. I could have seen that at the first glance and any, every detail." How could you possibly know that, sir, when you didn't keep any notes of the documents, you kept no list of the documents. It's not that you said they were similar but you said that they were identical. I want to try and understand how you are so certain that they were two identical sets of documents?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the following situation. I had copies and I had what you termed "the originals." I compared the one to the other right away. That's what I do. At the time I received the documents, I had nothing to compare them to, nor at the time. Now, it won't be difficult to put these documents side by side, compare the headers, the numbers, the stamp, and everything else -- or the author, for that matter. It tallies in every respect. There is the date. You can't have the same date in two different dates or any other changes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: -- in a single invoices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: -- because we may be talking at cross purposes here. So if I understand you correctly, it's not precisely how the question framed but what you compared was the documents that the OTP had collected, which was shown to you by Mr. Zivanovic, with the documents that Mr. Zivanovic provided you with; is that correct? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We compared the documents, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So these are the documents, though -- not the documents necessarily, and I'm not imputing there was any substitution, but what you compared was the documents currently held with the documents seized by the OTP; is that correct? Currently held by Mr. Zivanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: There were documents that were in our possession, earlier on. And we compared those to these documents and we realised that they were identical. There were no discrepancies, no new documents that the OTP had and we didn't, and so on and so forth. We established no discrepancies. The number and the type of the documents that we received, were the same as those other ones. Well, now had there been any discrepancy at all, I would have known; but there was none. I am certain about that. Had this been a new document, for example, that we had and the OTP didn't and, well, that's what I mean. We didn't notice that sort of thing at all and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that brings your testimony to an end, Mr. Mijatovic. Thank you for coming over again, and once more I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no documents.

utterances.text: All right. That's the declaration that -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's close the argument here. Yes, we would like you to tender those --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will make the list and provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, unless I -- in case I haven't made myself clear, the end of this whole procedure today, and the end of the discussion, basically brings us back to the main reason for which we recalled -- we asked this witness to be brought again. The consequence or the bottom line being that precisely these documents are essential; and they need to be in the record and not just being shown to the Prosecution or to the Bench just to have a look at them and make up our minds what was provided and whether they are accepted. utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Clearly if they are going to be in the record all parties need to see them and be in position to make submissions upon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour, and could I make one more observation, and the reason I've risen is we were the only other party to make some submission in response to the Prosecution motion. Presumably that motion is in effect moot now because we have made various legal submissions. They have not been ruled upon. We are not inviting the Court to rule upon them. They involved, I would concede a quite difficult and perhaps even complicated areas of law which do not need to be gone into bearing in mind the offer that Mr. Zivanovic has just made, but I just wanted to be clear about that. That in effect this exercise has circumvented, and I make no criticism of that fact, has circumvented the need for further consideration of the Prosecution motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have put it as clear as it could be. I mean, we don't need to decide the motion in the first place, and the documents are going to be in the record. However, if you wish to have a look at them, not just you but all the others, you of course are free to do that. And if you want, you are free to make submissions. You only have to ask, and you will be given the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So take your time, Mr. Zivanovic. I don't want you to shift your concentration now on other matters. So do it at your leisure and pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I didn't understand. Your Honours, I already said due to the fact that the Prosecution has all these documents, they provided it meanwhile in July or all of the year. I provide it both to the Prosecution and both to the Chamber and to all my colleagues from the Defence. But basically they are absolutely the same as the documents from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- collection just without an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you have already stated. Just let us have a look at them now and then you tender them formally, and the others, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's do it this way. You will disclose these documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the -- microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the ones that. Sorry, my apologies. You will disclose these documents, the ones that have been made available to you by your investigator, and these documents, the other documents, for comparison purposes, namely the ones that were disclosed by the Prosecution, in two separate bundles, you will disclose them to each and every one of your colleagues and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And for Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I mean it's taken for granted. After which, if anyone wishes to make submissions, you will have ample opportunities. That applies to any member of any Defence team as well as the Prosecution. Then we will have the tendering stage by which time you will have had enough opportunity to prepare yourself. Is it clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, if you wish to see them now Mr. Mitchell or Mr. McCloskey, of course you only have to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We would like to see them now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we have a short break. We'll have a short break. Any one of the Defence teams that wishes to have a look at them now can also do so. We'll have a break of -- next break was due at quarter to 6.00, so we can have it now. We'll have it now. We'll have 25 minutes now, and those of you who wish to avail themselves of the document please do so. We'll reconvene at 20 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All settled, Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. McCloskey, and others, about the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And also just before I forget Mr. Vanderpuye looked over the list of Borovcanin documents, and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. So those documents are admitted. Before I give you the floor, Ms. Fauveau, you filed a motion today for the addition, and your 65 ter list of part of disclosure consisting in video. This would relate to witness who is scheduled to testify on Monday. Is there any objection on your part, Mr. McCloskey, or do you wish to take time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objection from the other Defence teams? So there being no objection, the motion is granted. Next, Ms. Fauveau. How long do you think your ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should finish today, but I expect I will go to the final moment of this session, maybe a few minutes early. Your Honours, this case has been brought to court by the Prosecution. It is, therefore, to the Prosecution -- on the Prosecution that the burden of the proof lies. Defence has no obligation to supply any evidence. Innocence, any accused in this case General Miletic is presumed innocence, innocence need not be proven. Defence of General Miletic has, however, chosen to provide evidence to contribute to the quest for truth. These pieces of evidence will confirm in an incontrovertible manner, the innocence of General Miletic. Criminal responsibility is individual and personal. No responsibility can be established on the simple fact that one is a member of the Serbian people or the army of Republika Srpska. The responsibility of an individual cannot be established simply by belonging to the army of Republika Srpska being a General and occupying a specific function. The Prosecution has to supply evidence, evidence beyond reasonable doubt, that the accused has committed criminal crimes and committed them with a criminal intent. As for General Miletic, we consider such evidence does not exist. We will try and show -- we will show that General Miletic had no criminal intent and that he committed no acts which could be defined as criminal. This case has seen an allegation of a joint criminal enterprise. It is an interesting construct from the Prosecution's point of view, but a very dangerous one for justice as a whole. Indeed, there is a risk of confusing innocence and guilty persons. To avoid such a trap, we will have to examine evidence with great caution. Indeed, contacts, relationship between different individuals, do not, as such, mean that all these individuals are part of a joint criminal enterprise. In this case there is an obvious relationship between the different units and the different individuals, between the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska, the subordinate bodies, including the Drina Corps, and the brigade subordinated to the corps. This link alone cannot substantiate and cannot be used as a proof of a joint criminal enterprise. It is just the normal you structural organisation of an army and of the chain of command. The simple fact that individuals communicate, that they have contacts, cannot substantiate a joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, when an officer of the Drina Corps turns to General Miletic for a piece of information, it doesn't mean that General Miletic is part of the joint criminal enterprise. It simply means that he is doing his job. The criminal intention of General Miletic cannot be derived solely from the fact that General Miletic was called upon. What we have to try and establish is what General Miletic did and said. His deeds, and only his deeds and his intent, are vital in establishing or disproving his responsibility. In no instance should he be held accountable for acts committed by others. Much circumstantial and indirect evidence has been supplied in this case. We will show that these documents, testimonies, and evidence supplied by the Prosecution, a number has -- has led to a number of conclusions; and we will draw other conclusions from these elements, conclusions that are more likely and more reasonable. What charges has the Prosecution brought against General Miletic? Under paragraph 75 of the indictment, he is being accused of making life unbearable for the inhabitants of the enclave in that he drafted Directive number 7, signed by President Karadzic; and in that he took part in and helped the policy set out in Directive 7 to restrict humanitarian aid to the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa. He is also being charged with wanting to defeat the military forces militarily. This is a perfectly legitimate goal in a situation of war, and he is also being charged with wanting to control the movement of Muslim population out of the enclave. The basis for these allegations is the position that General Miletic held -- or would have held in 1995 in the army of Republika Srpska. We disagree slightly with the Prosecution as to the functions of General Miletic in -- in 1995, but as I have already said, whatever his job, whatever General Miletic's job, it is not sufficient to establish criminal responsibility. You also have to identify and prove criminal intent and deeds that substantiate such a criminal intent. To refute the Prosecutor's allegation, we will specify a number of things. First of all, the position in which General Miletic actually was in 1995. His role in drafting Directive number 7. The reasons justifying the policy of the army of Republika Srpska relating to the transit of the humanitarian convoys, the authorisation procedure for humanitarian convoys, and the role of General Miletic in relation to humanitarian aid. And also we will establish the general situation in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in the spring and summer of 1995, and the role General Miletic played in the events that unfolded in July 1995 in and around Srebrenica and Zepa. The Prosecutor alleges that General Miletic represented General Milovanovic when he was absent and that his representation covered -- was valid for a large part of 1995. The Prosecutor, however, was very vague in establishing the exact period of time when General Milovanovic was not at his post. We intend to prove you that in the first half of 1995, General Milovanovic was indeed present at the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army in Crna Rijeka. We also intend to prove that during that same time, when General Milovanovic was not in Crna Rijeka, he was not in western Bosnia, but specifically in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. Indeed, and a forward command post was established in Zvornik, and General Milovanovic spent some time there. Briefly, indeed, but long enough to know exactly the situation in the region, much better, indeed, than General Miletic would have known it as he was remaining in Crna Rijeka. We will also bring evidence to identify the specify role and function blamed by General Miletic within the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska when General Milovanovic was not there. We are not saying that General Miletic was not the chief of operations and training. Operations and training is indeed a body within the staff of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. We will, however, show that in discharging his duties, contrary to what the Prosecution claims, he was not involved in the military operations led by corps and brigades. Corps and brigades have their own officers in charge of operations which lead these operations. We intend to give proof of the way in which such operations are planned and conducted at the different levels of the hierarchy within the army of Republika Srpska. We hope to show that General Miletic could not and was not involved in the military operations, both tactical and operational, and that he was not involved in the activities of the army of Republika Srpska in Srebrenica and Zepa. We shall show that General Miletic had other obligations and duties within the staff of the VRS Main Staff and that even if he had wanted to do so, he could not cover and monitor each of the operations conducted by each of the corps and brigades on the frontline in Republika Srpska. The Prosecutor has tried to convince you that when General Milovanovic was not there, General Miletic stood in for him. We are not saying that when General Milovanovic was not there General Miletic was not standing in for him within the staff. But I must insist on the fact that he was only standing in for him in the staff and not in the Main Staff Command of VRS. We must draw a clear distinction between "staff" and "command." We shall bring evidence that will shed light on the way in which the Main Staff was organised so that no one may confuse "command" and "staff." This should also enable us to understand clearly where and when and in what function where General Miletic could stand in for General Milovanovic. We also intend to show that General Milovanovic's functions within the Main Staff Command of VRS was never discontinued even when he was in western Bosnia. Indeed, when General Milovanovic was not in a position to discharge some of his duties within command, some of these functions, contrary to the staff functions, were not transferred on to General Miletic but passed on to other generals serving within the Main Staff of VRS. Indeed, some of these functions were covered by General Mladic himself. According to the indictment, Directive number 7 is the beginnings of the JCE, which General Miletic would have taken part in. We shall give evidence relating to Directive 7 and we shall show that this directive is first and foremost a directive, a military act legitimate in and of itself. We are not denying the fact that General Miletic would have taken part in the drafting of the directive, or, more specifically, to the formatting of the directive. We shall show that the formatting of the directive, as is the case for any directive or any similar military act, is the usual -- forms part, rather, the usual duties of the officer in charge of operations. We shall present evidence concerning the operations within the Main Staff of the VRS and the decision-making process within its command structure. You shall hear General Maso, who drafted directive number 9. He will explain how a directive, an order, or any other military decision is thought through, drafted, and formatted. We hope that such evidence will help us understand precisely what role General Miletic played in the drafting of Directive 7. By identifying the specific role of General Miletic vis-a-vis Directive 7, we hope to show that there is no evidence attributing to General Miletic the infamous sentence incriminated in the indictment. This directive is not a directive of General Miletic. It is an act by the Supreme Commander, President Karadzic. If the Prosecution wants to prove General Miletic's responsibility vis-a-vis this sentence, he must show that General Miletic wrote it, and there must be no reasonable doubt that he didn't do so. We intend to show that there is no evidence than the incriminating sentence was thought or drafted by General Miletic. Why are we convinced that General Miletic did not write this sentence? We rely, indeed, to answer that question on the evidence that has already been supplied and the evidence that we shall supply. As I have said, the allegations of the Prosecutor based solely on the functions of General Miletic who would have stood in for General Milovanovic, and, therefore, would have been the main advisor to General Mladic. However, the Prosecutor has never indicated where General Milovanovic was in February, March 1995 at the time when Directive number 7 was drafted. We shall show that General Milovanovic was at his post at that time, his post as Chief of Staff of the VRS serving in the Main Staff of the VRS. He was not at the forward command post in western Bosnia, he was serving in the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka. As you have already seen, General Milovanovic has signed the transmission letter under which Directive number 7 was sent to the 1st Krajina corps. We shall give evidence that General Milovanovic did not only transmit Directive number 7 to the 1st Krajina Corps but also to the other corps. He personally signed this cover letter to the Directive number 7, to the Sarajevo corps, to the Herzegovina corps, and to the Drina Corps. You should learn that on the eve of sending Directive number 7 to the subordinate unit, General Milovanovic attended a lengthy meeting with President Karadzic. As Directive number 7 was being drafted in February, March 1995, General Milovanovic was indeed serving in the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka. He was discharging fully his functions as Chief of Staff of the VRS. He was available to advise General Manic and to make a contribution to the drafting of the infamous directive. We will also look about the reasons that brought about the drafting of Directive number 7. And we shall show that at the end of January 1995, the VRS had its annual meeting at which the commanders of the corps proposed tasks that they felt they could and should carry out during 1995. You shall hear that President Karadzic attended that meeting and set the tasks of the army down. We are not questioning the fact that officers -- that the officer in charge of operations has to format the directive as identified by the commander in its staff. However, we shall show that once the text has been drafted, the president, as Supreme Commander, as signatory of the directive, can bring final amendments and correction to the draft, the incriminating sentence, according to the indictment, can perfectly have been amongst the amendments and corrections brought by President Karadzic. We have all heard General Milovanovic say that he didn't remember Directive number 7 and that he had had no knowledge of it. We shall show you orders signed by General Milovanovic referring to Directive number 7. The orders that are built and founded on Directives number 7 and 7.1. These are not orders under the -- sent out under the authority of General Milovanovic but orders that he personally signed. We shall show also that the subsequent directives, Directives 8 and 9, relating more specifically to the western Bosnian front of which General Milovanovic was the commander in charge in July and August of 1995, refer directly to Directive number 7. We shall show that it is unthinkable that General Milovanovic had no knowledge of Directive number 7. We shall also show that in April and May 1995, General Milovanovic was monitoring on the ground the completion of tasks that he had set for the eastern Bosnian Corps and the Drina Corps. These tasks, more specifically operation Spreca derive directly from Directive from 7 and 7.1 and were drafted in the orders that I had referred to earlier. General Simic, the then-commander of eastern Bosnian [indiscernible], will discuss operation Spreca, the operation described in directives 7 and 7.1. General Simic will also describe the role of officers serving the Main Staff in this operation. Now, why am I mentioning General Milovanovic so much? Quite simply because the main piece of evidence for the responsibility of General Miletic as supplied by the Prosecutor is the alleged absence of General Milovanovic and the functions that General Miletic is supposed to have discharged in his absence. We shall show that this allegation from the period -- from the point in time in which the directive was drafted and until June is erroneous. Now, to avoid any misinterpretation, we are not saying as the Defence of General Miletic that General Milovanovic would be responsible for anything. We are just trying to show that as a subordinate to General Milovanovic, General Miletic cannot be held responsible for acts and decisions made at that point in time at the Main Staff and by the Main Staff of the VRS. Let us now move on to humanitarian aid. We are not saying that the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica wasn't difficult. We are not saying that there were no controls imposed to humanitarian convoys and there weren't any restrictions. However, we are not convinced that the humanitarian situation in the enclaves was the consequence and due to these controls and restrictions. Moreover, we deny the relationship between Directive 7 and the policy vis-a-vis humanitarian convoys. We also object to the existence of a specific policy of the VRS relating to the humanitarian aid bound for Srebrenica and Zepa. We object to the allegations made by the Prosecution, according to which General Miletic is meant to have had a key role in defining this policy vis-a-vis humanitarian aid convoys. Letting humanitarian aid go through is not an absolute right exercised unrestrictedly. Letting humanitarian aid through a territory -- through the territory of a party to a conflict and bound for the territory of another party to the conflict is bound by strict rules. It is not -- we are not talking of internal rules of the Republika Srpska but of international rules derived from the Geneva Conventions. Before we can -- before anyone can establish restrictive policy on humanitarian aid which would have made life untenable, we have first of all to establish that this humanitarian aid was being sent in accordance with international requirements or with the requirements of international humanitarian law, and that it was meant for the civilian population and used by the civilian population it was being sent to. We shall show to dispel any doubts that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina did all they could to maintain a difficult humanitarian situation in the enclaves. We shall show that the convoys supposedly transporting and conveying humanitarian aid in fact were laden with munition and weapons; and we shall show that humanitarian aid was in fact used in fact for -- to serve the needs of the Bosnia Herzegovina army. Captain Novakovic, an officer in the Drina Corps, and Maksimovic, an officer in the Zvornik Brigade will testify to that. Checking and controlling humanitarian aid is a right of the party to the conflict which is letting this convoy go through its territory. Should any humanitarian aid convoys be used to transport illicit wears, the party which authorises the transit is entitled to restrict humanitarian aid or even to cancel it in some extreme situations. We shall show that the authorities of Republika Srpska were founded in cancelling these convoys but never cancel them. However, they did try and enforce a number of rules, rules that should have been abided by. We hope to show that the policies of the Serbian authorities vis-a-vis humanitarian convoys, was the result of the type of products being conveyed in these convoys and of the abusive use to which these convoys were put by the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities. Indeed, they were being used for other purposes than humanitarian aid. You have already had an opportunity to show -- to see the evidence that these so-called humanitarian convoys, in fact, transported weapons and munition. We shall also show you that the actual humanitarian aid ended up in the warehouses of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army. Rather than being distributed to the civilian population this aid was distributed to the military units of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army. As for the restrictions to humanitarian aid in 1995 as imposed by the Bosnian Serb authorities, we know that the Prosecutor is arguing that this is the direct consequence of Directive number 7. We shall show that the restriction to humanitarian aid goes back much further. For simple reasons, the reasons I have exposed, these restrictions we want back to the beginning of the war, no specific changes intervened in the policy of the VRS after the adoption of the Directive number 7. We shall show that the situation in March, April, and May of 1995 was not different from the situation in January and February 1995. It was not different from the situation in 1994. We shall show that in the period following the adoption of Directive number 7, the amount -- the monthly amount of humanitarian aid arriving in Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves was the same as the amount arriving before the directive. And we shall show that the amount of humanitarian aid in the enclaves in April and May 1995 was the same as what it had been in April and May of 1994. We shall show that the transport of some wears was still forbidden and restricted and that these restrictions were unconnected with the military activities in eastern Bosnia in July of 1995 or with Directive number 7 and the alleged determination to making life unbearable for the civilian population. These restrictions were applied on all fronts and determined by perfectly understandable military reasons. Transport of freight and video cameras was generally band for quite simple reason. No army, even in time of peace, ever allows for its units or its equipment and materiel to be filmed or that pictures should be taken of it. Fuel was -- the passage of fuel was also limited from the very beginning of the war. You shall hear that humanitarian convoys moved more difficult -- difficulty -- with more difficulty when the relationship between the authorities of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR were tense. You will also hear that before Directive number 7 was adopted there were tense moments during which there was less humanitarian traffic than at some points in time after directive number 7 was adopted and before the transit of humanitarian aid was completely suspended. We shall also show that the restriction imposed to the convoys were unconnected to the Directive number 7 and that there was no specific policy adopted regulating humanitarian aid to the enclaves in eastern Bosnia. On the contrary, we shall give evidence that the enclaves in eastern Bosnia were better provisions in 1995 than other places. Lastly, we shall talk about the role played by General Miletic as regards humanitarian aid. The Prosecutor tendered into evidence those documents that had been sent to the subordinate units bearing the name of General Miletic. Providing a simplistic explanation of these documents, there was no reference whatsoever to the procedure applied to humanitarian convoys established well before Directive 7 by the civilian and military authorities of the Republika Srpska. We will concentrate on specifying the exact nature of these documents, as well as the information sent to the subordinate units. We will specify which procedure is applied before these documents were sent to that by the name of General Miletic. You will understand that these documents were something like a pass for the convoys, and without these documents, no convoy could go through. In fact, what is important are those decision that were taken upstream. The general decisions relating to the conditions of passage of the convoys and specific decisions relating to the passage of individual convoys; thus, determining which goods could be transported. As part of this trial, nobody has ever explained where and how and by who these decisions were taken. Even though the Defence does not need to adduce any proof of the innocence of the accused, we shall explain how this procedure worked, i.e., granting authorisation for the convoys to go through. Understanding this procedure is essential, for it will enable us to understand which role General Miletic played in the issue of humanitarian convoys. Witness Kralj, a staff officer who was working under the orders of Colonel Djurdjic, the latter having being the officer in charge of humanitarian aid in the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, member of the coordination body in charge of humanitarian aid will try to explain who took those decisions relating to the passing of the humanitarian and how these decisions were actually taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. What's this the witness's name, this last witness that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kralj, K-R-A-L-J. Thank you, Your Honour. You have heard the UNPROFOR generals, General Smith and General Nicolai [Realtime transcript read in error, "general in this case lie"] the commander and chief of staff of the United Nations forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995. They both mentioned those meetings held in the presence of the authorities of the Republika Srpska, including the Serbian military authorities. They confirmed that during the period relevant to the indictment, they had no occasion to meet or contact General Miletic. General Miletic did not attend the meetings in the presence of UNPROFOR. He was not the contact person of UNPROFOR at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. We will show that the procedure that applied to the convoys and the general policy adopted was addressed at these meetings which were attended by representative of UNPROFOR and members of the army of the Republika Srpska. General Miletic did not attend these meetings. You have, I am sure, already wondered how it is that these generals, a commander and a chief of staff of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not know General Miletic, the man who according to paragraph 51 of the indictment, purportedly played a central role in imposing restrictions on humanitarian aid. Part of the answer is already contained in the case file. General Nikolai explained that when a question of this kind arose the only answer could be provided by the generals. We will demonstrate that General Nikolai was right and that it is quite logical that neither General Nikolai nor General Smith had any dealings with General Miletic. General Miletic was colonel until June 1995 and had no power or authority to negotiate with the UN generals or to take any decision relating to the passage of the convoys. We will show you the documents, the orders, stemming from the army of the Republika Srpska, that indicate what general policy was adopted by the army as regards the convoy. All these orders -- none of these orders is an order issued by General Miletic. All these orders go back to the period where General Milovanovic, the chief of staff of the army of Republika Srpska was indeed present at the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska. And that these orders were not signed by General Mladic [as interpreted], they were signed precisely by General Milovanovic. But there is something even more important. We will show you how General Miletic did not decide which of the convoys or goods could pass. He signed the documents that were sent by their subordinate units indicating which convoys could pass and which had received authorisation from the authority in charge. The only connection between Miletic and humanitarian aid was precisely this document, i.e., information sent out to the subordinate units indicating that the decision had been taken by the authorities in charge on the basis of orders and previously established rules. We shall demonstrate that without this document the subordinate units could not have let the convoys go through and that these documents in no way be characterized as a contribution to the implementation of a policy applying to the passage of the convoys. Lastly, we shall talk about the situation in the area of the Drina Corps. The military operations that were conducted in the spring and in the summer of 1995, including July 1995; and the role played by the officers of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska during the operation -- during the military operation conducted in the area of the Drina Corps during this period. We have already discussed the presence of General Milovanovic in the area of spring of 1995. We hope to show that in May 1995 he took part or attended the meetings at the command of the Drina Corps and approved those decisions and plans and devised by this command. And after the departure of General Milovanovic who left for the Krajina no Drina Corps decision or plan was approved at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. We hope to demonstrate although that the separation of the enclaves was an ongoing task that had been given to the Drina Corps well before Directive number 7 was drafted; and that was per se, legitimate. Of course, we hope to demonstrate that the allegations made by the Prosecution concerning the role played by General Miletic in the military operations conducted in the area of the Drina Corps are incorrect. Paragraph 52 of the indictment mentioned the shelling of the enclaves and inter alia the shelling of the 25th of May, 1995. The Prosecutor alleges that the Predunaci [phoen] brigade shelled Srebrenica on the orders of the Main Staff of the Drina Corps. Even though we did hear about this shelling on the 25th of May 1995, we have never seen a single order sent by the Main Staff, and we hope to demonstrate that on the 25th of May, 1995, General Miletic certainly did not issue or forward such an order and that he was in no way involved in what was going on in Srebrenica. His immediate superior, General Milovanovic, was at the time in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska at Crna Rijeka. According to paragraph 53 of the indictment, the attack of the observation post Echo of the UNPROFOR was a prelude to the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. We will demonstrate that what the Prosecution calls or qualifies as an attack on the Echo post was in fact not connected to operation Krivaja; but it was a secondary operation that had been triggered by the situation on the ground and probably had been requested by the local civilian authorities. Witness Milenko Jevdjevic will testify about this. We will also discuss the events in Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995 and the role played by, or rather, the absence of General Miletic in these events. When we talk about the events in Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995, it is important to emphasize the very special position General Miletic had in this trial. He is the only accused who went neither to Srebrenica nor to Zepa whether it be before, during, or after the military operations in these areas. Admittedly, the criminal acts can be committed without the person or the perpetrator being physically present; however, we would like to draw your attention to the distances because in this particular case distance is of the essence. Distance between where General Miletic was and where these criminal acts were committed. Because of -- General Miletic did -- had no direct knowledge of what was happening on the ground. He relied on the reports provided to the Main Staff. And if these reports were erroneous, his perception was also erroneous. We will demonstrate that this is precisely what happened in July 1995. Pursuant to paragraph 75 of the indictment, General Miletic is accused of having monitored the Muslim forces during and after the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa. The surrender of the Muslim forces after the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa, the activities of the units of the army of the Republika Srpska in the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. And he is accused of having controlled the moment when the Muslim population moved out of the enclaves. We hope to prove that no officer can monitor and control such activities from a distance. Surveillance and control are tasks which can only be conducted on the spot, where things are happening. Throughout this entire trial, the Prosecutor has tried to convince us that General Miletic was a key man, the advisor to General Mladic, who was coordinating everything that was going on. He purportedly has been the coordinator throughout the entire period of 1995 and also in July of 1995. We have already indicated that we will adduce evidence confirming that General Milovanovic was at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska in Crna Rijeka in the first half of July 1995. And we will now focus our attention on July 1995. You have heard that General Milovanovic was not there at the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska at Crna Rijeka in July 1995. We do the not challenge that. However, you have heard also that General Milovanovic was indeed there and attended the lunch hosted in honour of General Milovanovic in July 1995. General Milovanovic does not deny that he was during the entire period of 1995 Chief of Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska; and we shall show that he was permanently at General Mladic's disposal. He could be contacted at any time and be consulted as required. If General Miletic were to replace him at the staff of the Main Staff, there will be no reason for him to replace him along side General Mladic, and we will show that he never replaced him in any position that goes beyond that of a position in the staff of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. But let's take it a step further. The Prosecutor alleges that General Miletic must have been at the Main Staff headquarters, because in his position he was coordinating and centralizing everything, liaising between General Mladic, his assistants, and subordinate units. We will show that this was not the role played by General Miletic and that he never had such authority. We know that General Mladic was on the ground and in Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995. We will also show you that General Miletic as officer in charge of the operations should have gone -- accompanied General Mladic if he had been, in one way or another, involved in these operations. In July 1995, in Srebrenica, in Zepa General Mladic did not need a go-between. Did he not need a go-between for he was there himself, he was there along side General Krstic and could give his orders directly. As far as the connection between him and President Karadzic and the reports that were sent to him that I allege in paragraph 75 (b) and (c) of the indictment, we would show that these reports cannot, per se, constitute a criminal act. The drafting of these reports was the daily task and regular tasks of the body in charge of such operations. These reports, daily reports, did indeed describe what the situation on the ground was, but this description was not the result of the observation on the ground made by General Miletic but based on the reports of the Main Staff that he received. Evidence will show that these reports were neither contacts nor the main links between President Karadzic with the army of Republika Srpska nor the main source of the information he received regarding the situation on the ground. The reports that were sent to President Karadzic in July 1995 bore the name of General Miletic. They bear his name, but not his signature, and the Prosecutor has never proven that he had, in fact, signed these documents during the relevant period. Why is this signature important? This signature is important because in July 1995 during the military operation in and around Srebrenica, General Miletic could not have signed these reports because he was not at the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska in Crna Rijeka. He was in Belgrade where his daughter was on the 10th of July 1995 celebrating her 18th birthday. You will hear testimonies of her daughter and other people who attended the birthday party thus confirming that General Miletic learned about the entrance of the army of the Republika Srpska into Srebrenica when he was in Belgrade. We will show that before going after Belgrade, General Miletic did not know that the army of the Republika Srpska was going to enter Srebrenica. He could not know that because the order given to enter the enclave was given on the 9th of July 1995; and we will show that on the 9th of July 1995, General Miletic was in Belgrade with his family. In July 1995, whatever his knowledge may have been about the military operations conducted by the Drina Corps, if ever he did know anything, he was not concerned by this. He had left for Belgrade. He had been allowed to go to Belgrade, and he had been allowed to leave because his presence at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was not required, not needed. And admittedly, General Miletic returns on the 12th of July, 1995, and is at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. He is there. But what does he do, how does he behave and what are his intentions? What does he know about the events that were unfolding in Potocari? We will show that General Miletic did not take part in any way in what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa in the summer of 1995 and he could in no way influence these events. We will also show that when General Miletic came back to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska in Crna Rijeka he did not receive any reliable information concerning the situation on the ground. His understanding of the knowledge -- of the situation was quite approximative. All he could have known is that the Muslim civilian population had been evacuated to Potocari in the direction of the territory under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but each officer of the army of Republika Srpska, each officer of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, knew that also at that time. So this knowledge, per se, has no significance. In July 1995, General Miletic was not in Srebrenica; he was not in Bratunac; he was not in Potocari either. Did he not attend those meetings at the Hotel Fontana. He not know what the position of the DutchBat was. He not what the representatives of the Muslim community wanted or did not want. We will show that General Miletic didn't -- could not know and did not know what the conditions were in Potocari. He could not know, either, under which circumstances the evacuation had taken place; and we will stress this as far as General Miletic is concerned. What is important is not what actually happened in the field but what perception General Miletic could have had since he was not there and at no time did he go there. When these military operations were being conducted in Zepa, General Miletic was still in Crna Rijeka. He was not in Zepa. He was not attending the meetings in the presence of the representatives of the Muslim populations. He did not attend the meetings with the UNPROFOR members. We do not deny the fact that General Miletic may have been informed about these meetings. He may have known that an evacuation of Zepa was being negotiated, but we will show that it's precisely because he knew that the evacuation was being negotiated because he knew that the UNPROFOR representatives and other international organisations were involved, that he could reasonably think that these evacuations -- that he could not reasonably think that these evacuations could contain the seeds of a criminal act. You know that General Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Miletic"] was in Zepa, as was General Tolimir and that these negotiations were taking place in Zepa also. We will show that all the decisions were taken in Zepa, and that General Miletic and the other officers in Crna Rijeka were involved. Neither involved in any military operation or the avocation of Zepa. General Obradovic, who was the immediate subordinate of General Miletic came back from sick leave on the 17th of July 1995 and as of the 17th of July 1995 onwards, together with General Miletic, was at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, Crna Rijeka. We'll say that the officers at the staff at Crna Rijeka, in concluding, General Miletic, we'll talk about what they knew about Zepa. We will show that in July 1995, the only information that General Miletic had about the situation in Srebrenica and Zepa was information that was communicated to him in those reports--

utterances.text: No I'm fine --

utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, and just slow down a little bit. I mean, I was assuming all the way that they had a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 85, line 5, it should read "General Mladic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will show that in July 1995, the only information that General Miletic had on the situation in Srebrenica and Zepa was the information that had been forwarded to him in those reports he received. Taking delivery of the reports does not show in any way that there is a criminal intent. This was a part of his daily tasks. In addition, we have every intention of proving that those reports he received in July 1995 were insufficient, inaccurate, and sometimes vague. Admittedly, the army of Republika Srpska was organised and structured, and the reports were sent by the subordinated units. However, we will adduce evidence showing that the materiel situation was difficult, that the equipment of the Republika Srpska was not the best in the world, that there were technical failings and other problems, and that the reports were not always so accurate. General Miletic had information which was sent to him. He had no direct knowledge of these events. He did not influence them in any way, and he could not influence them in any way. We do not deny that the task of General Miletic was to follow the situation on the front lines in Republika Srpska, but we insist on the term "follow." For following does not mean monitoring or controlling. The terms "monitor" and "control," contrary to the term "follow" involve an active role. We will show there is a difference between these terms and we will prove that General Miletic did not play an active role. General Miletic was not there to influence the situation on the front but forward to General Mladic in as reliable a fashion as possible the information he had received. We will also show that the major concern of General Miletic in July of 1995 was not the eastern Bosnian front. General Mladic was there, and General Miletic was of no help to him, for as far as that was concerned, General Mladic knew the situation much better than did General Miletic. Since General Mladic had more information than General Miletic on the eastern Bosnian fronts, he did not need General Miletic to inform him about anything concerning the situation in eastern Bosnia. However, he did need General Miletic to provide him with information about the situation on the other fronts, i.e., the fronts in the areas of the 1st and 2nd corps of the Krajina, the Sarajevo Corps, the eastern Bosnian corps, and the Herzegovina Corps. And it was this task that General Miletic devoted himself essentially to in July of 1995. We will show that what is important is not the Main Staff of an army per se, but the command that is located there. When the command and -- the commander and his closer associates are not at the Main Staff, decisions were not taken in Crna Rijeka, but it is where the commander and the command were. The fact that General Miletic remained in Crna Rijeka when the entire command was elsewhere does not show that he was important. Quite the opposite. This fact ascertains that General Mladic did not need General Miletic to take his decisions. That said, we do not want to undermine the role and position of General Miletic in the army of the Republika Srpska. We wish to acknowledge his due role. His role was important in the running of the army, but the army of the Republika Srpska was not, per se, a joint criminal enterprise; and any contribution to the running of it was not criminal either. What is important, and this is what the Prosecutor needs to prove beyond any reasonable doubt, are criminal intent and acts that contributed to the commission of crimes. We will show that these evidence does not exist because General Miletic did not in any way participate or contribute to the tragic events of the Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, sorry. I just thought it would perhaps be easier now. utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. Then that would make more sense. I just wanted to bring this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There are further names and things missing, but I am sure they will be taken care of. Do you have a witness present, shall we start with him now or?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's bring the witness in, please, and start him off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good evening, and welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned by the Defence team for General Miletic. Before you start giving evidence, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be testifying the truth. Text had just been hand to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn making with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Madam Fauveau will be asking you some questions. I need to advise you on -- or Mr. Petrusic. I need to advise you that it's very unlikely that we will finish with your testimony today or tomorrow. Today we have only got 15 minutes, but I don't envisage that we will finish tomorrow either. So you will be here and -- over the weekend and then continue on Monday. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And good evening, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the outset, for the record please state your name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Obradovic, born on the 13th of January, 1950 in Visegrad, Republika Serbia [as interpreted], Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Republika Srpska, Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us about your background in terms of education, both civilian and military?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The first eight forms of elementary school, that was in Visegrad. In 1968 or rather from 1968 to 1972, the military academy for the ground force in Belgrade. After that between 72 and 77, I served in the school for reserve officers, infantry, in Bileca. Between 1977 and 1980, or rather 1988, I served in Belgrade. Having completed the staff command school for tactics, I was deployed to the Derventa garrison, and I served there as Chief of Staff of the 327th Motorised Brigade. After Derventa, once the war had begun, I was transferred to the Main Staff. It was in the 1st of September, 1994, that I reported to the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka. I then became chief of the operative department for training and operations of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. I remained in that position until the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What were your duties before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war I was platoon commander in the school for reserve officers and company commander at the military academy for ground forces. I taught firing lessons to soldiers at Derventa, of the 327th, I was Chief of Staff and also deputy commander. And there were two further six-month cycles. In addition to my regular duty as Chief of Staff, I also performed the duties as commander of the 327th Motorised Brigade, because the commander, Colonel Rejiceva Surevic [phoen], had retired on account of his age. These were the duties that I performed before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, when the war broke out, which rank were you holding in Derventa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Main Staff in September 1994, what was the rank you held at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior when you came to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of training and operations, Colonel Radivoje Miletic. He was a colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you stay in that position at that place throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, I remained chief of the operations department, but I had different duties. All along the front line at different points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 5D1039. Your Honour, Mr. President, there will be a whole succession of documents now. Therefore, there is a binder that has been provided with all these documents in it. The OTP have had a chance to inspect the documents and no objections were raised about any additions or anything like that. This is simply for ease of handling and in order to make it more convenient for the witness during his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's hear Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We have no objections, but perhaps for clarification, my notes indicate that he was the chief of operations and training under Miletic, who was chief of operations and training. So that can't be right. So I don't know if there is a translation issue or something else going on. We also don't have -- I don't see any history from 1991, 1992, 1993. If that was -- if it was there, I didn't catch it. So just that might help clarify before we start getting into documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Obradovic, let us first remove any doubt -- or, rather, let's take this in chronological order. Your war biography, between 1992 and your arrival at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, I was Chief of Staff and also deputy commander of the 327th Motorised Brigade at Derventa. I remained in that position until another commander was appointed, and that was before I arrived at the Main Staff. Do you want to know about the deployment of the units or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe this is quite sufficient for our purposes. Thank you. What about 1994, the 1st of September. You say you came to the Main Staff on that day. Please, sir, give me a chance to finish my question. Thank you. What was the duty that you performed when you came to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the operations department, and this was part of operations and training, that department, and the department was headed by Colonel Miletic. I was in the operations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I am not sure if this is sufficient for the Prosecutor's purposes in terms of distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I see Ms. Fauveau on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a problem in the translation. The witness was chief of head of operations but General Miletic was chief of administration for operations and training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Mr. Petrusic, we have five minutes left. Just want you to make sure that you can deal with something useful in these five minutes, otherwise we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am about to move on to documents that may require more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I thought, and so that's why I intervened. We stand adjourned until tomorrow. Mr. Obradovic, we will continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. In the meantime -- in the meantime you are not to discuss with anyone or allow anyone to discuss with you the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.
